chapters.title: Chapter 4: Beyond Percentages: Control, Rights and Exits

lessons.title: Secondary Sales and Buybacks: Taking Some Money Off the Table

children.text: At the Series B, Meera's 6,000 shares are worth ₹34.2 crore on paper. She is also on a founder's salary, has a home loan application she cannot support, and has not taken a holiday in four years. Paper wealth pays for none of that. This lesson is about the two ways a founder converts a slice of ownership into money before an exit, and the rules that decide whether either is available to you.

body.text: A founder who has taken a little money off the table makes better long-term decisions than one who has not. The goal is not to cash out. It is to remove the pressure that makes you accept a bad exit.

children.text: Primary and Secondary Are Different Transactions

markDefs.definition: A sale of existing shares by an existing shareholder to a buyer. The money goes to the selling shareholder, not to the company, and no new shares are created.

children.text: Every round so far in this course has been primary: the company issues new shares and receives the money. A
is the opposite. Nothing new is issued, the share count does not change, and the money goes to the person selling. The cap table changes hands rather than growing.

columns.label: Primary
points: The company issues new shares
Money funds the business
Total share count rises, everyone is diluted
Needs a board and shareholder approval and a return of allotment

columns.label: Secondary
points: An existing holder sells shares they already own
Money goes to the seller personally
Total share count is unchanged, nobody is diluted
Needs a transfer deed, board approval and any consents in the shareholders' agreement

children.text: How Much a Founder Can Realistically Sell

Investors are not against founder liquidity, they are against founders losing motivation. In practice that means secondaries become available from around the Series B, are usually limited to a small slice of a founder's holding, and are often bundled into a primary round so the incoming investor buys both new and existing shares. Meera sells 600 of her 6,000 shares, which is 10% of her holding.

stats.label: Shares sold
stats.context: 10% of her holding, at the ₹57,029 round price

stats.label: Net of capital gains tax
stats.context: Before surcharge and cess, at current unlisted long-term rates

children.text: Gross: 600 shares × ₹57,029 = ₹3,42,17,400. Cost of acquisition: these were founder shares issued at ₹10 face value, so 600 × ₹10 = ₹6,000. The capital gain is therefore ₹3,42,11,400, essentially the whole amount.

Shares in an unlisted company held for more than 24 months are long-term capital assets, taxed at 12.5% without indexation. Tax = 12.5% of ₹3,42,11,400 = ₹42,76,425, leaving about ₹2.99 crore before surcharge and cess, which apply on top. Check current rates and holding periods with your chartered accountant, because both have changed in recent years.
Her ownership: 6,000 minus 600 leaves 5,400 shares out of an unchanged 35,071, so 15.40% instead of 17.11%. No other shareholder's percentage moves at all, because no new shares were created.

body.text: Secondary shares often sell below the primary round price. The buyer is purchasing ordinary shares with no liquidation preference, no anti-dilution and no information rights, so a discount of 10% to 25% to the round price is common. At a 20% discount Meera's 600 shares fetch about ₹2.74 crore gross rather than ₹3.42 crore. Ask what price your secondary is being struck at before you agree to the number of shares.

children.text: The Consents You Need Before Selling a Single Share

body.caption: What stands between you and a secondary sale

cells: Existing investors can buy the shares on the same terms before an outsider does
Other shareholders may insist on selling a proportionate number of their own shares alongside yours
A founder share transfer is usually a reserved matter, so consent is needed whatever your percentage
A private company's articles restrict transfers. The transfer is executed on Form SH-4 with stamp duty paid and the register of members updated
FEMA and the applicable pricing guidelines
A sale by a resident to a non-resident must not be below fair value, supported by a valuation, with reporting to follow
Unvested shares cannot be sold, and some agreements bar founder sales entirely before a stated round

children.text: The Other Route: A Company Buyback

Instead of finding a buyer, the company itself can buy shares back and cancel them. This is how many Indian startups have given employees liquidity, and founders sometimes participate too. It is heavily conditioned under Section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013, and the tax treatment changed materially in recent years.

columns.label: Secondary sale
points: A third party or existing investor pays you directly
No company cash is used, so runway is untouched
Share count unchanged, nobody is diluted
Proceeds are taxed as capital gains in your hands

columns.label: Company buyback
points: The company uses its own funds and cancels the shares
Spends cash the business might need, so investors scrutinise it
Share count falls, so remaining holders' percentages rise
Conditions under Section 68 apply, and buyback proceeds are now taxed as dividend income in the recipient's hands

body.label: The buyback tax shift
body.value: Taxed as dividend, not capital gains
body.context: Amounts received on a buyback are now taxable in the shareholder's hands as dividend income, at their applicable slab rate, rather than being taxed in the company's hands. That change makes a buyback far less attractive than a straight secondary sale for many sellers. Confirm the current position with your chartered accountant before choosing a route.

body.text: Size the sale carefully, because it is read as a signal. Selling 5% to 10% of your holding says you are de-risking. Selling 40% says you no longer believe the biggest outcome is ahead, and investors in your next round will hear it that way. Agree the number with your board in advance, and be able to explain what the money is for.

body.title: Your stake after a secondary
body.prompt: Meera holds 6,000 of TiffinBox's 35,071 fully diluted shares and sells 600 in a secondary. No new shares are issued. What is her fully diluted stake afterwards? Answer to two decimal places.
body.explanation: 5,400 ÷ 35,071 = 15.40%, down from 17.11%. Note that the denominator does not move: a secondary changes who owns the shares, not how many exist, so no other shareholder is diluted by her sale.

body.title: Name the first hurdle
body.textWithBlank: A clause letting existing shareholders buy your shares on the same terms before you can sell them to an outsider is called a right of first ___.
body.explanation: A right of first refusal, usually paired with tag-along rights, is the first thing to check in your shareholders' agreement before you line up a buyer.

body.title: Which route, and why?
body.question: A profitable Coimbatore SaaS company has ₹12 crore of cash it does not need for operations. Two founders want ₹4 crore between them, and an existing investor is willing to buy their shares at the last round price. Which route is usually better for the founders?
options: A company buyback, because using company cash avoids involving an investor
A secondary sale to the investor, because it leaves company cash in the business and the proceeds are taxed as capital gains rather than as dividend income
Neither, because founders cannot legally sell shares before an exit
A buyback, because it increases every remaining shareholder's percentage
body.explanation: A secondary keeps ₹4 crore of runway inside the company and is taxed as capital gains in the founders' hands. A buyback spends company cash, must satisfy the Section 68 conditions, and the proceeds are now taxed as dividend income at slab rates, which is usually the worse outcome for a founder with other income.

body.title: ₹5 crore, three ways
body.scenario: You co-founded a Bengaluru fintech six years ago and hold 19% of a company last valued at ₹450 crore. Your Series C investor is willing to buy ₹5 crore of founder shares as part of a round closing next month, at a 15% discount to the round price. The company also has ₹40 crore of cash and healthy reserves. Your shareholders' agreement gives existing investors a right of first refusal on any founder transfer, requires investor consent, and caps founder secondaries at 15% of a founder's holding per round. Your co-founder does not want to sell anything.
body.prompt: How would you approach this, and what would you check first?
body.modelAnswer:
What to check before anything else:
1. The cap. Your agreement limits you to 15% of your holding per round, so first confirm that ₹5 crore fits inside it at the discounted price. If it does not, you either sell less or negotiate a one-time waiver as part of the round.
2. The right of first refusal. Existing investors must be offered the shares on the same terms. This is procedural rather than fatal, but it takes time, so start it early in the round timetable rather than at closing.
3. Vesting and leaver clauses. Only vested, unrestricted shares can be sold. Six years in this is probably fine, but check.
4. The price. A 15% discount to the round price is within the normal range for ordinary shares without preference or information rights. Ask whether the discount can narrow if you sell fewer shares.
5. Tax. Unlisted shares held beyond the long-term holding period attract long-term capital gains tax, with surcharge and cess on top, and your cost base as a founder is close to zero. Model the net figure with your CA before agreeing the gross.

How to approach it:
1. Take the secondary rather than pushing for a buyback. It leaves the company's ₹40 crore inside the business, avoids the Section 68 conditions, and is taxed as capital gains rather than as dividend income.
2. Sell a modest slice and say why. A founder selling roughly a tenth of their holding after six years, with a stated purpose, is a normal conversation. Frame it to your board before it becomes a rumour.
3. Do not pressure your co-founder. Different founders have different obligations, and an investor buying from one founder and not the other is perfectly normal. Make sure the round documents do not force symmetry you have not agreed.
4. Ask for the team to be included. If the investor has appetite, extending the secondary to employees with vested options is one of the highest-return goodwill decisions you can make, and it strengthens your next hiring conversation.

body.title: Running a founder secondary properly
steps: Confirm how many of your shares are vested and free of any lock-in or leaver restriction.
Read the transfer clauses: right of first refusal, tag-along, investor consent and any cap on founder sales.
Agree the size with your board in advance and be ready to explain the purpose.
Establish the price, including any discount to the round price, before agreeing the number of shares.
Model the tax and net proceeds with your chartered accountant, using your actual cost of acquisition.
If the buyer is a non-resident, confirm valuation and pricing compliance and the reporting that follows.
Execute the transfer on Form SH-4 with stamp duty paid, get board approval and update the register of members.
Ask whether employees with vested options can be included in the same secondary.

cards.definition: A sale of existing shares by a shareholder, where the money goes to the seller and no new shares are created.
An issue of new shares by the company, where the money funds the business and all existing holders are diluted.
The right of existing shareholders to buy shares offered for sale on the same terms before an outsider can.
The right of other shareholders to join a sale and sell a proportionate number of their own shares.
A purchase by the company of its own shares, which are then cancelled, subject to the conditions in Section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013.
The reduction from the primary round price at which ordinary shares typically change hands in a secondary.
What you originally paid for the shares, deducted from sale proceeds to compute the capital gain.

points: A secondary sale transfers existing shares, so the seller gets the money and nobody is diluted.
Founder secondaries usually become available from the Series B and are limited to a small slice of a holding, often bundled into a primary round.
Meera selling 600 of 6,000 shares at ₹57,029 raises ₹3.42 crore gross and takes her from 17.11% to 15.40%.
Secondary shares often price 10% to 25% below the round price, because they carry no preference or investor rights.
Rights of first refusal, tag-along rights, investor consent, transfer formalities and non-resident pricing rules all sit between you and a sale.
A company buyback is the alternative, but it spends company cash, must satisfy Section 68 conditions, and proceeds are now taxed as dividend income in the recipient's hands.
Size the sale so it reads as de-risking rather than as a loss of belief, and agree it with your board in advance.
Where possible, extend liquidity to employees holding vested options in the same transaction.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not legal, tax or investment advice. TiffinBox Foods and the other companies and people described are fictional, and all prices, share counts and proceeds are illustrative. Capital gains rates, holding periods, surcharge and cess, the tax treatment of buyback proceeds, the conditions in Section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013 and FEMA pricing and reporting requirements all change over time and depend on your facts. The tax figures shown ignore surcharge and cess. Consult a qualified chartered accountant, company secretary or lawyer before selling any shares or approving a buyback.
